Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-29
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Rohit Patel (CTO), Dana Morales (Infra), Samantha Lee (ML)

Optional auto-summary:
Summary: Initial latency + streaming readiness discovery. CedarBridge needs 95th percentile latency ~ < 300ms for short responses, streaming for token-by-token updates, and burst concurrency up to 120 concurrent sessions during peak. Interested in Hosted for fast start, Dedicated for SLAs and predictable throughput, and possible Private (VPC) for compliance. Redwood to run benchmarks with CedarBridge corpus.
Topics: p95 targets, streaming token/sec, concurrency, KV cache, batching, VPC, SOC2, pricing.
Action items: see metadata.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, we, we have about 40 minutes — quick intros?
[00:08] Rohit Patel: yeah hi this is Rohit, CTO at CedarBridge, we've got Dana who runs infra and Samantha who owns model infra, uh we're trying to understand how Redwood could fit into our production inference for conversational analytics.
[00:18] Maya Chen: awesome, thanks. Liam, want to intro yourself?
[00:22] Liam O'Connor: yeah hi I'm Liam, SE on the inference team, I focus on throughput and latency profiling, streaming, batching, quantization tradeoffs — happy to walk through benchmarks.
[00:31] Dana Morales: thanks. quick context — we currently run a mix of managed API and in-house Triton endpoints, we get okay throughput but streaming is noisy and p95 spikes during business hours, our latency budget for short responses is around 250–300ms p95.
[00:46] Samantha Lee: and we have a use case that streams partial transcripts to client apps, token-by-token, so the tail matters more than average. also we have bursts up to ~120 concurrent interactive users during reports.
[00:58] Maya Chen: perfect, that's exactly the sort of constraints we typically help with. to confirm: p95 target 300ms for short responses, and streaming with smooth token/sec — do you have expected tokens per second and sequence lengths?
[01:12] Rohit Patel: typical messages are 20–40 tokens, but sometimes we have larger 200–400 token summaries for batch jobs. For streaming sessions it's often 1 token per 50ms at peak in the browser, but server-side we want to push as fast as possible. token/sec target maybe 60–200 depending on model.
[01:32] Liam O'Connor: okay, that helps. two axis here: per-request latency (p95) and token throughput for streaming. For smaller messages, a lot comes down to model size, kernel selection, and cold vs warm KV cache. On Hosted we have warm pools and prefix caching which helps p95. For Dedicated you get pinned GPU pools with predictable latency.
[01:52] Dana Morales: we care about isolation — data residency and logs, so Private/VPC is interesting, but we need to understand the perf delta vs Hosted.
[02:02] Maya Chen: totally. generally, Hosted gives fastest ramp and predictable performance for most workloads, our Dedicated clusters give you reserved capacity and tighter SLOs, Private can be configured inside your VPC but the network overhead and customer-managed infra can add variability — we can quantify that in benchmarks.
[02:18] Samantha Lee: are your p95 measurements token-level or response-level? how do you measure streaming p95?
[02:25] Liam O'Connor: good question. Our p95 is response-level end-to-end — for streaming we also measure time-to-first-token and inter-token spacing. For streaming smoothing we look at p95 of first-token latency and p95 of the 90th token spacing, etc. That gives you both tail and jitter.
[02:42] Rohit Patel: can you run with our tokenization? our tokenizer splits some of our legal text into long tokens so that affects throughput.
[02:49] Liam O'Connor: yes, in the runbook we'll include a tokenization script so we can reproduce exact token counts. we prefer you send a small corpus of representative inputs.
[02:57] Maya Chen: and we typically run three benchmark modes: short interactive (20–40 tokens), mid-length (150–400 tokens), and summary batch (400+). we'll report p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and cost per 1k tokens for each model/quantization setting.
[03:14] Dana Morales: what about KV cache and streaming? we rely heavily on context windows and we do a lot of re-queries where prefix caching would save us.
[03:22] Liam O'Connor: prefix/KV caching is one of the biggest wins for re-use patterns. On Hosted we have automatic prefix caching that pays off for repeated contexts; for Dedicated you can configure longer-lived kv caches and batch windows. On Private you can run the same runtime but caching parameters depend on your deployment.
[03:37] Samantha Lee: latency numbers you said earlier about <300ms p95 for short replies — what models and hardware do you expect for that?
[03:44] Liam O'Connor: for 20–40 token outputs, you can hit sub-300ms p95 on an A100/80GB or H100 depending on model family — if you use an optimized open model with int8 or q4_k_m quant, or our curated smaller family we verify, it's achievable. For large LLMs with 70B+ params, the numbers change — there the p95 might be 400–800ms unless you use faster hardware or distillation.
[04:04] Rohit Patel: we prefer open models to avoid ref vendor lock, but we need production-grade SLAs. what are typical differences in cost & latency between Hosted and Dedicated?
[04:14] Maya Chen: Hosted will show slightly better latencies out of the gate because we manage warm pools and routing optimizations, but Dedicated reduces cost per token at scale and you get reserved capacity and stronger throughput guarantees. We'll include a cost-per-effective-token table in the pricing scenarios.
[04:30] Dana Morales: network details for Private: do you need cross-account VPC peering, or can we host the inference nodes in our subnet?
[04:37] Liam O'Connor: for our Private option we support customer-managed subnets and can deploy the inference runtime into your VPC with peering/privatelink. We'll provide a network checklist — usually need NAT, egress rules for metrics, and options for KMS/HSM integration for key management.
[04:54] Samantha Lee: curious about batching — you mentioned continuous batching earlier, how does that affect latency spikes? we saw spikes when batches align poorly.
[05:02] Liam O'Connor: continuous batching is designed to reduce per-token cost while controlling latency. We adapt the batching window based on workload — if you have latency SLO of 300ms we cap batch windows to a few ms for short requests and allow larger windows for throughput-optimized paths. You can set policies to prioritize latency over cost.
[05:20] Rohit Patel: do you expose those policies in config or is it managed?
[05:24] Maya Chen: it's exposed — we have routing and autoscale policies in the Console. You can set latency targets, cost thresholds, and fallback models. For Dedicated you can pin model variants, and for Private you get the same config surface but applied to your cluster.
[05:38] Dana Morales: on compliance — SOC2 and audit logs — how long of retention do you offer for logs on Hosted? and for Private?
[05:45] Maya Chen: Hosted default retention is 90 days for operational logs, with add-ons for extended retention. We can provide audit logs exports for SOC2. For Private, logs are customer-managed so retention follows your policies. We'll include the SOC2 report and our compliance pack.
[05:59] Samantha Lee: one practical: when you do streaming, do you do chunked HTTP/2 or web sockets? we need low jitter in browsers.
[06:06] Liam O'Connor: we support chunked HTTP/2 and server-sent events, plus websockets for persistent sessions. For browser jitter we recommend keeping connection warm and using smaller chunk sizes and local smoothing on the client.
[06:18] Rohit Patel: ok. for the benchmark, we want to run a simulated production traffic pattern — burst to 120 conc, steady 30 conc off-peak. can you reproduce the bursts?
[06:27] Liam O'Connor: yes we can. we'll run both steady-state and burst runs. For Dedicated we'll allocate a reserved GPU pool sized to meet your 95th percentile at the target model/config, e.g., X GPUs for 120 concurrent sessions at 20–40 tokens, we'll show you utilization curves.
[06:42] Maya Chen: rough timeline for the benchmark: if you can share the sample corpus and tokenizer by Friday, Liam can run initial single-node profilers early next week and we'll schedule a 2-hour dedicated run after that.
[06:52] Rohit Patel: sounds good. anything else on security or pricing caveats?
[06:57] Maya Chen: just that for Dedicated we have commit tiers — if you want a 99th percentile SLA for availability and latency we can discuss enterprise terms. Also note that quantization (int8/q4) can affect determinism so we'll include quality regressions checks.
[07:13] Dana Morales: do you have a recommended QA for quantized models? we can't accept hallucination regressions.
[07:18] Liam O'Connor: yes we tie quality monitoring to prompt sets/evals. Our Optimize tool suggests quantization profiles and flags regressions against your eval suite. We'll surface difference metrics and equivocation.
[07:30] Samantha Lee: any gotchas with token accounting — do you bill partial tokens on streaming? how do you compute cost per interaction?
[07:37] Maya Chen: billing is per token consumed/generated; for streaming we aggregate tokens at the end of session. We can provide estimates per-interaction given your avg token lengths.
[07:46] Rohit Patel: competitors — we ran tests with Anthropic and self-hosted Triton; their streaming was ok but the tail was inconsistent. how do you compare?
[07:55] Liam O'Connor: Anecdotally Hosted Redwood often beats managed endpoints on p95 for streaming because of our warm routing and caching, Dedicated beats self-hosted in predictability because we run tuned kernels and autoscaling. We'll include a competitive note, but we'll focus on empirical numbers from your runs.
[08:10] Maya Chen: ok let's walk through the concrete deliverables — Liam, runbook outline?
[08:14] Liam O'Connor: sure: 1) tokenization script and corpus ingestion 2) profiler runs for single-request latency and token throughput 3) burst simulation for concurrency 4) Dedicated sizing run 5) report with p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, cost-per-1k tokens, and quality metrics. We'll also capture network RTT effects for Private.
[08:33] Dana Morales: will you measure end-to-end from our browser or from an internal load generator? we want e2e numbers.
[08:38] Liam O'Connor: we'll capture both: a loadgen that hits the inference endpoint inside the same region to isolate infra, and an e2e browser-simulated run that includes client network. We'll separate the numbers.
[08:49] Samantha Lee: what's the expected deliverable timeline?
[08:52] Maya Chen: if corpus arrives Friday, profiler Monday, scheduled run Wednesday, report by Friday — so roughly two weeks to an initial report.
[08:59] Rohit Patel: that works. can you also include a price estimate for a 3-month pilot?
[09:04] Maya Chen: yep we'll include Hosted vs Dedicated pilot pricing and a Dedicated commit example for steady-state.
[09:11] Dana Morales: small nit: when we talk about p95 of 300ms is that for first token or full response? we need both sometimes.
[09:18] Liam O'Connor: we will report both: first-token p95 and full-response p95. For streaming-first token it's usually lower since generation dominates inter-token spacing later.
[09:28] Rohit Patel: any network tricks to reduce jitter? we have CDNs in front of clients.
[09:32] Maya Chen: keep the inference close to clients with region routing and use connection pooling; avoid unnecessary proxies in the path; for Private we can co-locate inference nodes in your subnet to reduce hops.
[09:43] Samantha Lee: would you recommend starting on Hosted then moving to Dedicated?
[09:46] Maya Chen: that's the common path — Hosted to validate, then Dedicated to optimize for cost and SLAs, and Private if you need VPC/on-prem constraints. We'll map scenarios.
[09:55] Rohit Patel: ok let's close with next steps.
[09:58] Maya Chen: recap: Rohit will send corpus + tokenizer by Friday; Liam will prepare runbook and initial profiler by Monday; Maya will send pricing scenarios and compliance pack; schedule a 2-hour Dedicated run next Wednesday. Any blockers?
[10:11] Dana Morales: none, thanks.
[10:13] Samantha Lee: none.
[10:14] Rohit Patel: great, appreciate it.
[10:16] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the runbook.
